Fields:

Commentary:
At Alder Park Oval in Southgate, Eastport chose to bat first in a match that never settled into one clean rhythm, because every time they looked ready to turn a useful passage into control, Ridgeway found a wicket or a quiet spell that dragged the innings back toward them. Noah Grant went early, pinned by Finn Carter before the batting side had built any kind of base, and that should have left Eastport cautious, but Caleb Rivers refused to let the innings shrink. His forty-nine from thirty-six balls was the first real statement of the day, full of quick hands, hard cuts, and two lifted shots that forced Ridgeway out of an easy new-ball squeeze. Isaac Wells played the quieter hand beside him, and their stand of sixty-five turned a nervous start into something workable. The issue for Eastport was that the innings never found a second partnership of the same weight. Harry Blake removed Caleb before the damage became larger, then later returned for Isaac and Ethan Vale, which meant Eastport kept losing the batters who might have given the innings continuity. Owen Sinclair, the captain, did the most important holding work through the middle, making forty-five from sixty-eight balls and keeping the card alive through stands with Liam Cross, Ethan Vale, and Mason Cole. Liam’s seventeen briefly added punch, Ethan’s thirteen took up time, and Mason’s fifteen gave the lower middle a little motion, but Ridgeway kept breaking the innings before it could become a proper closing platform. Miles Turner was the bowler who gave the first innings its final shape. He removed Liam, then Owen, then Julian Pike, and finally Sam Reed, finishing with four wickets and ensuring that Eastport’s last ten overs produced more strain than acceleration. Ryan Brooks was left not out on seven, but the tail had little room left by then, and Eastport closed on one hundred and eighty-two in the forty-sixth over. That total had substance because Caleb Rivers attacked and Owen Sinclair anchored, but it also carried regret because Eastport were one hundred and forty-six for five with overs left and still could not stretch the innings beyond a mid-range target. Ridgeway’s chase began with enough order to make the target look manageable. Nathan Doyle and Oliver Hart put on forty-seven, Nathan playing the cleaner attacking hand while Oliver supplied the stability. Dylan Foster removed Nathan, Owen Sinclair took out Isaac Bennett, and Oliver was then run out by Ryan Brooks, so Ridgeway suddenly found themselves sixty-seven for three with the chase still very much alive. That was where Callum Reed became the match’s central figure. Marcus Flynn gave him the first serious lift, striking thirty-one from twenty-seven balls in a stand of forty-nine that restored momentum and pushed Ridgeway past the hundred mark. Mason Cole removed Marcus at one hundred and sixteen, and the chase again had room to wobble. Samuel Cross then stayed long enough for a thirty-two-run stand, though that passage was heavily padded by wides and no-balls, a detail Eastport will not enjoy reading because a defending side with one hundred and eighty-two cannot keep donating release runs when wickets are still possible. Ryan Brooks eventually removed Samuel, and when Owen Sinclair bowled Jacob Hayes at one hundred and fifty-eight for six, Eastport had one last opening. Another wicket there could have made the match tense. Callum closed that door. Henry Shaw came in, played a simple unbeaten eight, and let Callum control the finish. Callum’s fifty-eight not out from seventy-eight balls was not a wild innings; it was the innings that stayed attached to every pressure point. He rebuilt after sixty-seven for three, absorbed the Marcus Flynn wicket, carried the extras-heavy middle passage, survived the sixth wicket, and then scored seventeen of the final unbeaten stand to take Ridgeway home. Eastport’s bowlers had meaningful moments: Owen Sinclair’s two wickets and tidy spell kept pressure in the chase, Mason Cole bowled ten disciplined overs, Dylan Foster struck first, and Ryan Brooks had Samuel Cross. Their problem was control between wickets. Twenty-five extras, including twenty-two wides, softened almost every squeeze they created. Ridgeway were not flawless, but they were more connected across the full match: Miles Turner and Harry Blake held Eastport below a bigger score, the top order gave the chase a platform, Marcus Flynn restored the tempo, and Callum Reed carried the match through every late complication. Ridgeway reached one hundred and eighty-three for six, won by four wickets, and qualified because they had the one batter who refused to let the chase lose its main thread.
